claims.text: Preheating the build plate to 200–400 °C during laser powder bed fusion of high-entropy alloys reduces thermal gradients.
Build-plate preheating reduces residual stresses in additively manufactured high-entropy alloys.
Build-plate preheating improves dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defect density relative to an unheated baseline.
The proposed intervention is substrate preheating at 200–400 °C immediately before and throughout the build.
The intervention is applicable to laser powder bed fusion of high-entropy alloys having similar melting ranges.
A stably and uniformly heated substrate and an inert atmosphere for oxidation control are required operating conditions.
Reduced in-process thermal gradients minimize residual stresses and hot-crack formation during solidification and cooling.
Preheating raises the initial temperature of deposited layers and lowers temperature differences between layers during melting and solidification.
Reduced thermal gradients limit strain localization.
Reduced thermal gradients limit porosity formation.
Limiting thermal gradients and strain localization produces fewer microcracks, less warping, and better interlayer bonding.
Preheating will lower porosity and hot-crack density relative to an unheated build.
Preheating will improve net-shape accuracy relative to an unheated build.
Preheating will increase ultimate tensile strength and yield strength by approximately 10–20% relative to an unheated build.
Standard laser powder bed fusion without substrate preheating has higher residual stress than the proposed preheated process.
Standard laser powder bed fusion without substrate preheating has greater porosity and dimensional inaccuracy than the proposed preheated process.
The proposed effect may not apply to alloys that are highly sensitive to aging or require specific post-build heat treatments.
The cited evidence does not directly document the effect of substrate preheating on additively manufactured high-entropy alloys.
Additively manufactured CoCrFeNi has exhibited intergranular hot cracks with high residual stresses near those cracks.

A lack of improvement within experimental error in dimensional accuracy, defect reduction, and mechanical properties for a 300 °C preheated build relative to an otherwise identical unheated control would falsify the hypothesis.
